questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The method of binding steel and coal
questions.learningObjective: identify the reconciling purpose of the first supranational authority
questions.stem: In 1950 a minister proposed placing the coal and steel of several states under one authority holding powers none of the member governments had held before. What was the method meant to achieve?

options.text: Making the material of war too scarce for any two states to arm and attack, so war defeats itself

options.misconception: confuses a control on two inputs with a general commercial monopoly
options.text: Giving the authority a monopoly on trade, so imports fell and every producer earned a protected price

options.misconception: assumes equal costs across states, which is not what a common authority provides
options.text: Fixing one coal price across the group, so industry in every state costs the same to operate

options.misconception: turns a production authority into a lender, which is what recovery aid had been
options.text: Funding loans for reconstruction, so that states borrowed once instead of competing for lenders

questions.explanation: Two states that have fought three wars in a generation have in common the ability to build guns, so an authority that sets how much steel leaves each side and where it goes takes away the means of a quick war, and because the constraint is material and enforced by a body neither side controls, a sudden quarrel cannot undo it. The tempting answers turn the scheme into a trade monopoly, a common price list, and a lending facility, none of which is what placing an industry under a supranational authority does.
questions.hint: Ask which physical shortage removes the ability to start a war, not just the will to start one.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Choosing the first industry to place under a common authority
questions.learningObjective: evaluate which first step least endangers the whole design
questions.stem: A delegate argues that the whole design collapses if its first step sets off a fight, and asks which industry should therefore come first under a common authority. Which choice carries the least risk of an argument?

options.text: Steel, because tanks and guns are made from it and a shared mill cannot be turned on one side alone

options.misconception: assumes an uncontroversial sector, when cloth rules divided producers in every member state
options.text: Textiles, because cloth is the cheapest good to supervise and the least likely to offend any state

options.misconception: calls credit uncontroversial, when control of credit is what governments guard most closely
options.text: Banking, because credit is a matter of arithmetic and needs no political agreement at all

options.misconception: treats farm policy as obviously popular, when it is the sector that splits member states
options.text: Agriculture, since farms are numerous and any rule about them pleases a wide majority of voters

questions.explanation: The criterion is not which sector is easy to regulate but which one has the smallest political cost of being regulated, and steel wins on that test because the states that most feared a common authority were exactly the states with the largest steel interests, so binding that one industry both removed the war-making capacity and forced the objectors to accept the arrangement from inside rather than by defeat. The tempting answers pick sectors that look uncontroversial on paper and were in practice the ones that divided producers and governments most sharply.
questions.hint: Ask which sector's rule would be objected to most strongly, and why that helps here.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A vote lost inside the common authority
questions.learningObjective: analyze what a supranational council changes for a dissenting state
questions.stem: The 1951 treaty created a council in which the member states held votes but a measure did not require each government's separate agreement, and the delegates of one state have just been outvoted on a price. What follows for that state?

options.text: It must comply, so a dispute over steel can be settled without stopping the whole authority's work

options.misconception: reinstates a veto the treaty deliberately took away from a single member
options.text: It may withhold agreement, since the measure takes effect only once every state has consented

options.misconception: adds a national ratification step the council was set up to avoid
options.text: It must send the measure to a national parliament, since the council may only recommend a decision

options.misconception: makes a decision wait for a further debate that the voting rule was designed to avoid
options.text: The measure is delayed until the next session, since the council cannot act without a general debate

questions.explanation: The whole point of pooling the industry was to substitute a majority for unanimity in a sector where one state had previously blocked everyone else, so a state that dislikes a price can be outvoted but cannot hold the authority hostage, which is the difference between a working rule and a freeze. The tempting answers restore a veto, insert a national parliament, and require a further debate, each of which returns the authority to the condition it was built to escape.
questions.hint: Ask what the voting rule was made to replace, and who it was written to disempower.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A common market built around farm policy
questions.learningObjective: explain why agriculture was placed at the centre of the bargain
questions.stem: The 1957 treaties created a common market for goods and a single policy for farm prices and support. Why did the same treaties put agriculture at the centre of the bargain?

options.text: Farm incomes varied so sharply that the agricultural states would not join a market without support

options.misconception: assumes a rule about equal volumes, which a common market never imposed
options.text: Food had to be shared equally, so every state was bound to import the same quantity of grain

options.misconception: converts a distributive payment into a favour bought by the number of voters
options.text: Agriculture employed most of the voters, so the policy was simply a concession to a large electorate

options.misconception: claims farm inputs were all domestic, when trade was the whole problem the market addressed
options.text: Farming used nothing bought from abroad, so it was the one sector a common market could leave alone

questions.explanation: A market exposes each member's producers to competition from the others, and the states whose farmers were small, poor, and politically powerful could not accept exposure without a guarantee, so a common agricultural policy was the price of their signature on a market they would otherwise have blocked. The tempting answers turn the policy into an equal-share rule, into an electoral purchase, and into a sector untouched by trade, none of which explains why the policy had to be common rather than national.
questions.hint: Ask which member states would have been most exposed by an open market for farm goods.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: An empty year after one state walked out
questions.learningObjective: explain why unanimity allowed the community to seize up
questions.stem: In 1965 a head of state refused to sign the community's medium-term budget and withdrew his representatives from its meetings, and for a year the institution did almost nothing. Explain why the machinery seized up.

options.text: Every decision needed each government, so one refusal over one budget stopped the whole programme

options.misconception: assumes the rules gave one head of state personal control, which they never did
options.text: The rules gave the head of state a personal hold on the budget, so he could stop the body alone

options.misconception: confuses a dispute about the level of spending with a dispute about who may block it
options.text: The members simply wanted a larger budget, so the year's disagreement was about wanting more money

options.misconception: dismisses the freeze because the sums were small, though the budget funded the whole market
options.text: The budget was too small to matter, so the year cost nobody anything and the talks simply drifted

questions.explanation: A rule that lets any participant stop everything converts one government's objection into paralysis for all the others, and because the budget is the instrument that pays for the market rules, a refusal to approve it freezes not merely that line but the machinery built on top of it, which is the institutional lesson the following settlement answered. The tempting answers invent a personal power, reduce the crisis to wanting more money, and dismiss a budget that funded the market itself.
questions.hint: Ask what the missing signature blocked, and then what it blocked in turn.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Majority voting on one seat per state
questions.learningObjective: explain what the compromise of 1966 corrected
questions.stem: After the year's crisis the members agreed that many decisions would be taken by qualified majority in a council where each state had one vote. What problem was that rule designed to remove?

options.text: A single seat had been enough to freeze everything, so a qualified majority ended the hold-up power

options.misconception: assumes votes were counted by population, which the one-seat rule explicitly was not
options.text: Votes had been counted by population, so the small states needed a rule giving each of them a veto

options.misconception: reads a change in voting power as a change in meeting frequency
options.text: The meetings had lasted too long, so the rule was really about how often the council should meet

options.misconception: turns a procedural rule into a ceiling on spending that the members did not impose
options.text: The budget had been spent too quickly, so the rule was designed to limit total commitments

questions.explanation: The crisis proved that a rule requiring everyone's assent gives the smallest objector a veto over the whole institution, so requiring only a qualified majority, together with one vote each to keep the large states from dominating, changes a single objection from a stop into a dissent, which is what lets the market keep moving. The tempting answers invent a population count, a meeting schedule, and a spending limit, none of which the crisis concerned.
questions.hint: Ask what one state could do to the whole body under the old rule.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A government reverses its position on membership
questions.learningObjective: explain why a state's calculation about joining changed
questions.stem: A government that had twice declined the European community applied for membership within a year of the oil price shock and a change of prime minister. What best explains the reversal?

options.text: Its economy fell further behind its partners, so staying outside had become the more expensive choice

options.misconception: credits a single interest group, where the government's own calculation was national
options.text: Food prices rose sharply, so farmers organized and forced the government to apply on their behalf

options.misconception: assumes a currency agreement came first, whereas a common currency came much later
options.text: It had already agreed a common currency abroad, so the application only recognized a done deal

options.misconception: denies a change of position, which the application itself records as a reversal
options.text: The government had never opposed entry, since the earlier refusals belonged to another party entirely

questions.explanation: Entry is a bet on relative performance, and when a shock hits a trading partner abroad harder than the state in question, the comparison of living standards and growth that had justified staying out reverses, so the same economy that once had nothing to gain now has a market it cannot easily reach from outside. The tempting answers hand the decision to one organized interest, claim a currency agreement that came decades later, and deny a reversal the application itself records.
questions.hint: Ask what the shock did to this state relative to the states inside the market.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Joining after a change of regime
questions.learningObjective: recall the stated condition for membership
questions.stem: One country whose government had been in the hands of a military council until 1974 became a member of the European community in 1981. What made it eligible in the way the other members were?

options.text: Restored civilian rule after the council fell, which met the community's stated entry condition

options.misconception: assumes a size threshold for membership, which the treaties never set
options.text: Its size and population, which supplied the votes needed to reach a qualified majority in council

options.misconception: makes naval reach an entry condition, which the treaties nowhere list
options.text: Its navy, which guarded the eastern sea lanes the community's southern members depended upon

options.misconception: invents a founding claim by a country that joined thirty years after the others
options.text: Its long colonial history, which gave it a claim to be treated as a founding member of all

questions.explanation: The community's stated condition was stable civilian government, and a state that had spent a decade under a military council could not meet it until the council fell and elections were restored, so the date of entry follows the date of that restoration rather than any economic or strategic consideration. The tempting answers invent a size threshold, a naval requirement, and a founding claim for a country that joined long after the group was formed.
questions.hint: Ask which of the entry conditions the country could not meet until 1974 had passed.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A long list of decisions moved to majority vote
questions.learningObjective: interpret an act summary as an answer to a blocking problem
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1986 act records that a long list of decisions may now be taken by qualified majority in a council where each state holds one vote, and that the commission becomes answerable for enforcing the market rules. Which crisis is the act answering?

options.text: Years of agreement by all had let any one state hold up the market, so a voting rule was required

options.misconception: reads a voting reform as a spending cut, which the summary nowhere mentions
options.text: The community had overspent on its budget, so the act's purpose was to reduce total spending

options.misconception: assumes a dissolution, where the act rebuilds the market rules instead
options.text: The members were about to leave, so the act rebuilt the structure they were about to abandon

options.misconception: inverts the direction of the change, from the commission back to national parliaments
options.text: The commission had grown too strong, so the act returned the market rules to the national parliaments

questions.explanation: The single market cannot be enforced by a rule that one state can refuse, so moving a long list of decisions to a qualified majority and making the commission answerable for enforcement attacks the two reasons a market had not finished being built, namely a unanimity rule and rules nobody was obliged to police. The tempting answers turn the act into a budget cut, a rescue of a community about to break up, and a reduction in central power, each of which runs against what the summary records.
questions.hint: Ask what a market needs in order to be real, and which of those two things the act supplies.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Completing the economic and monetary union
questions.learningObjective: explain why money and foreign policy were harder than a market
questions.stem: The 1993 treaty set out to complete an economic and monetary union, to add a common foreign and security policy, and to settle who would decide what. Why was that harder than the single market it followed?

options.text: A market only removes duties at a border, but money and foreign policy touch powers no state will cede

options.misconception: reverses the order of difficulty, since duties are settled by binding rules
options.text: The market was the harder step, since the duties were already gone and nothing was left to agree

options.misconception: asserts a settled outcome where the treaty was precisely an unfinished negotiation
options.text: Money and foreign policy were settled long before, so the treaty only recorded decisions already taken

options.misconception: claims nothing was added, when the treaty created a currency and a foreign policy
options.text: The treaty added nothing, since a single market had already required every state to surrender sovereignty

questions.explanation: Removing a duty at a border leaves the government's freedom intact, since it still decides everything inside its own territory, whereas one currency means giving up the ability to set interest rates and devalue to answer a shock, and a common foreign policy means a government can no longer act alone in a crisis, so the treaty had to bargain about who decides and how a state can still protect itself. The tempting answers reverse the order of difficulty, call the outcome settled when it was not, and claim the earlier stage required the same surrender.
questions.hint: Ask what a government keeps after the duty is removed, and what it gives up when the money is shared.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The objection to one currency across many budgets
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the strongest form of the fiscal objection to a common currency
questions.stem: Economists warn that a single currency across states with their own budgets and debts cannot be made to work unless someone is responsible when one state cannot pay. What is the strongest way to state that objection?

options.text: One rate must serve many economies, so someone must stand behind the weakest or it sets the terms

options.misconception: describes a fixed intra-group rate, which is exactly what a common currency abolishes
options.text: A common currency still needs a daily rate between the members, since trade never settles in one money

options.misconception: assumes one state issues the notes, which is the opposite of how the bank is built
options.text: Only one state may print the notes, since a shared currency requires a single national issuer

options.misconception: converts an argument about risk into a right of withdrawal the rules do not grant
options.text: A large surplus state must be able to withdraw, since the currency only works if it can be left

questions.explanation: One rate, one bank, many budgets means that a state in trouble cannot devalue or raise its own rates to recover, so if the currency's survival depends on that state, everyone else has an interest in its debt and no one state is willing to carry that burden alone, which is why the objection ends in a demand for a shared backstop rather than in any rule about printing or about exit. The tempting answers describe a system of floating intra-group rates, a single national issuer, and a right to leave, none of which is the problem being described.
questions.hint: Ask what a state cannot do for itself once the money is shared, and who pays for that.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Moving the rates inside the band in 1992
questions.learningObjective: explain why the strongest economy moved last
questions.stem: In 1992 the exchange rates inside the fixed band had to be realigned, and the largest and strongest economy resisted until it had to give way. Explain why that economy was the last to move.

options.text: Its currency had risen on export strength, so keeping the old rate priced its goods out of the others

options.misconception: calls the strongest economy the weakest, which is what the objection to a fixed rate requires
options.text: Its economy was the weakest in the band, so a fixed rate was the only way it could pay for imports

options.misconception: claims a non-membership the band's own membership contradicts
options.text: The band covered only small currencies, so the largest economy was never actually inside it

options.misconception: assumes one bank sets the band, where the rates are fixed by agreement among all
options.text: Its central bank fixed the rate for the whole band, so the others had nothing left to adjust

questions.explanation: A fixed rate is a promise that a currency will not adjust, so the economy whose currency has been pushed up by strong exports is asked to hold a rate that makes its own goods dearer than its partners' precisely when it is selling them best, and the price of moving is that the advantage unwinds, which is why the strongest economy resisted longest. The tempting answers call it the weakest member, deny it belonged to the band at all, and give its bank a power the agreement does not create.
questions.hint: Ask which economy benefits most from its currency being strong, and what the fixed rate takes away.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The conditions attached before a state may adopt the currency
questions.learningObjective: recall why entry conditions precede the common currency
questions.stem: Before any state could adopt the common currency it had to show that inflation, its budget balance, its debt, and its interest rates had stayed close to the best performers in the group. What is the point of those conditions?

options.text: One rate and one bank can only serve economies that behave alike, so the tests check for likeness first

options.misconception: assumes a fixed adoption date, which the conditions deliberately avoided
options.text: They fix the year in which every state must adopt the currency on the same day as its neighbours

options.misconception: reads convergence conditions as an order of entry, which is a different mechanism
options.text: They decide the order of entry, so the largest economies join first and set the terms for others

options.misconception: asserts a transfer of debt that the conditions never promised to any state
options.text: They move national debt onto the community, so any state that qualifies may spend more freely

questions.explanation: A common money and a common rate-setting body cannot manage economies whose inflation and borrowing differ wildly, because the shock the bank has to absorb is then a shock to the whole currency, so the conditions are a test of similarity rather than a promise or a queue. The tempting answers invent a common adoption date, an order of entry, and a transfer of debt, none of which is what a set of economic tests does.
questions.hint: Ask what a single interest rate does to a state that borrowed at a very different rate.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A statute on the bank that sets the interest rate
questions.learningObjective: interpret a statute summary as an institutional design
questions.stem: An original summary of a 1998 statute records that the bank's governors serve fixed terms, cannot be dismissed by any government, and set the interest rate without instruction from anyone. Why was that arrangement chosen?

options.text: No single government could be trusted with the money, so the bank answers to none of them alone

options.misconception: assumes the bank follows elected governments, which the statute's terms deny
options.text: The bank must follow elected governments, since only they are answerable to the people affected

options.misconception: gives the bank a price objective, which no central bank is instructed to pursue
options.text: Fixed terms exist to keep prices high, since rising prices protect the savings of savers

options.misconception: treats a newly shared function as the recovery of an old national one
options.text: Governments had already lost the right to issue notes, so the bank simply took over a vacant post

questions.explanation: Once the money is common, the rate that one government would set becomes a decision that raises or lowers prices for every other member, so the only arrangement that survives national disagreement is a body with fixed terms that no single government can dismiss, which is independence bought with the agreement to accept a price stability goal in return. The tempting answers make the bank accountable to one set of voters, hand it a target of high prices, and describe the reform as the filling of a vacancy the states had never lost.
questions.hint: Ask whose price level is raised by a rate decision once the money is shared.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Decisions taken where no voters elect anyone
questions.learningObjective: analyze the legitimacy complaint about the institutions
questions.stem: A critic says the community's decisions are made in a council and a commission that national voters elect no one to, and that a government in a large member state finds those decisions hard to reverse. What is the objection?

options.text: Authority sits where no electorate can dismiss it, so national parliaments lose control of policy

options.misconception: equates a body of member states with rule by a single power, which is a different claim
options.text: The decisions are made by unelected officials, so the community is an empire rather than a union

options.misconception: denies the presence of national parliaments the complaint is precisely about
options.text: National parliaments sit on every council, so any voter can dismiss every decision at once

options.misconception: accepts the accountability claim and disputes only the timetable
options.text: Voters are consulted before every vote, so the real complaint is how long the process takes

questions.explanation: A rule that the people elect a body to make, revise, and abolish is what holds a government to account, and when the decisive rules are made by a council and a commission that no national electorate appoints, the national parliament can complain but cannot reverse, so the objection is about the location of authority rather than about the empire label. The tempting answers substitute a different charge, deny that national parliaments are absent, and accept the accountability claim while disputing only speed.
questions.hint: Ask which body could undo a decision if a government disliked it.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two accounts of the largest enlargement
questions.learningObjective: synthesize external and internal causes of one enlargement
questions.stem: Two original summaries of the mid-1990s enlargement say different things caused it: one credits the eastern bloc's collapse, which left neutral states without a reason to stay apart, the other credits the union's own success, which made membership worth seeking. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: The eastern bloc's collapse removed the reason for neutrality, and the union's success made entry worth seeking

options.misconception: makes the two accounts mutually exclusive, when they describe different moments of one change
options.text: The two are rivals, since one makes entry pointless and the other makes it compulsory to seek

options.misconception: denies the eastern bloc's collapse, which the first summary takes as its given
options.text: Only the second summary applies, since the eastern bloc continued in the same form afterwards

options.misconception: denies any attraction, which the second summary's whole argument consists of
options.text: Only the first summary applies, since membership brought nothing a neutral state had been missing

questions.explanation: A state stays neutral while the reason for neutrality exists, and when the reason disappears the state's calculation changes from necessity to preference, and then the question is whether there is anything to prefer, so the second account supplies the attraction that the first one's changed conditions made possible. The tempting answers set the two against each other, deny a collapse both summaries assume, and deny the attraction the second account is made of.
questions.hint: Ask what a neutral state does once the reason for being neutral is gone.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: An expansion that multiplies rules and languages
questions.learningObjective: explain the institutional problem an expansion creates
questions.stem: The union's largest expansion added ten states at once, most of them former members of the eastern bloc, and the number of official languages, currencies, and legal traditions in force grew with them. What problem did the expansion create for the union?

options.text: Institutions built for a few members had to be rebuilt, since the rules outgrew the machinery

options.misconception: assumes the newcomers refused the rules, which membership itself obliged them to keep
options.text: The new members refused to apply the rules, so the single market built over decades was lost

options.misconception: makes the obstacle a shortage of money, which expansion makes easier rather than harder
options.text: The expansion cost too little, so the union could not staff the posts that guarded its outer border

options.misconception: invents a loss of seats that the enlarged councils and votes expressly provided against
options.text: The older members lost their seats, so the expansion threatened their share of the budget

questions.explanation: A decision-making structure designed for six assumes a small number of languages, a short list of legal traditions, and a manageable agenda, so an expansion that multiplies all three makes the machinery of agreement the bottleneck, which is why enlargements have been followed by rebuilds of how the union votes, legislates, and pays for itself. The tempting answers claim the newcomers broke the rules they had signed, that the expansion was too cheap, and that the older members lost seats the new arrangements were designed to protect.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the union's machinery was built for a handful of members.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Keeping one currency and one set of border controls out
questions.learningObjective: evaluate why partial membership can lead to exit
questions.stem: A state that kept its own currency out of the common one and kept its border controls out of the common arrangement later votes to leave the union entirely. What best explains how partial membership became a step towards leaving?

options.text: Opting out of what voters disliked made leaving read as a way of keeping what they valued

options.misconception: claims the opt-outs satisfied voters, which is the opposite of what triggered the vote
options.text: The opt-outs satisfied everyone, so the vote to leave came only after a change of taste in cooking

options.misconception: denies any benefit from membership, which the state's decades inside the union contradict
options.text: The state had gained nothing from membership, so the opt-outs merely postponed a decision already made

options.misconception: claims the parliament was abolished, which the opt-outs in fact preserved
options.text: Opting out ended national debate, so the vote to leave was taken with no parliament in session

questions.explanation: Opting out is a bargain in which a government promises voters they will keep the parts they value while the union proceeds, and once the costs of staying grow the bargain breaks, and leaving then looks to a voter like the only way to hold on to the currency, the market, and the trade agreements rather than lose them together, which is what turns a negotiated exception into an exit. The tempting answers claim satisfaction, deny any benefit from four decades of membership, and invent the abolition of a parliament the opt-outs left in place.
questions.hint: Ask what a voter expects to keep if the state leaves, and whether the opt-outs ever promised that.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A bank's losses become the currency's problem
questions.learningObjective: explain how a national banking failure became a currency crisis
questions.stem: A bank in one member state financed property loans that stopped being repaid, and the strain spread to that state's debt, to its banks in other members, and then to the currency as a whole. Explain how one bank's problem became the currency's problem.

options.text: One currency is one pool of confidence, so a bank's losses became a question about the money itself

options.misconception: assumes separate national note issues, which the single currency had already ended
options.text: Each state issues its own notes, so a loss in one state should have stopped at that border

options.misconception: asserts a common lender that the single currency does not create
options.text: The banks shared one lender, so the spread proves the crisis began in a common institution

options.misconception: asserts a guarantee the treaties never made, which is why the crisis was so severe
options.text: The treaties guaranteed every bank's debts, so no single state could have failed on its own

questions.explanation: A single currency means holders in every member hold the same claim on the same system, so a bank that cannot pay is not a local failure but evidence that the claims may be worthless, and depositors and investors have no separate national note to move into, which is why a national loss became a run on the money and required a lender no member would agree to provide on its own. The tempting answers assume national note issues, invent a common lender, and assert a guarantee the treaties never contained, which is the absence the crisis exposed.
questions.hint: Ask what a holder of the money does when a bank inside the system cannot pay.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rule that action belongs as close to the citizen as possible
questions.learningObjective: explain what the subsidiarity principle governs
questions.stem: A principle written into the treaties says that decisions should be taken as close to the citizen as possible and that the union should act only where the member states cannot act well alone. What does that principle do?

options.text: It sets the level at which action belongs, so the union is confined to what states cannot manage

options.misconception: turns a rule about levels of government into a rule about money
options.text: It sets the level of spending, since the principle is really a rule about how much each state gets

options.misconception: turns a rule about competence into a rule about who may vote in the council
options.text: It defines who may vote, since the principle decides which states sit in the council and which do not

options.misconception: invents a timetable for enlargement, which the principle nowhere addresses
options.text: It sets the timetable for enlargement, since new members may join only after a fixed delay

questions.explanation: The principle is a boundary on competence: where a national government can do the job adequately, the union has no business doing it, and where a single state is too small or too weak the union may, so it answers the complaint that decisions were being taken too high without denying that any common action is needed. The tempting answers convert it into a spending rule, a voting rule, and a timetable for new members, none of which it is.
questions.hint: Ask which level of government is the principle defaulting to, and against what test.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A note on states that pay and states that receive
questions.learningObjective: interpret a budget dispute as a two-way bargain
questions.stem: An original summary of a negotiating note records one state paying far more into the shared budget than it receives, another receiving more than it pays, and the two rejecting each other's account of who benefits. What makes the bargain possible at all?

options.text: Payments run in both directions, so no state can claim that it alone carries the common cost

options.misconception: calls the sums trivial, when the budget funds the market rules and the commission
options.text: The amounts are far too small to matter, so the dispute is only symbolic and costs nobody anything

options.misconception: assumes a veto by payers that the budget rules have never granted
options.text: Only the paying state votes on the budget, since payment is the test of who has a real stake

options.misconception: assumes payments are fixed, where the periodic agreements exist to change them
options.text: Payments are fixed by law forever, so the argument has no legal route to a settlement at all

questions.explanation: A budget in which every state paid and none received would be a tribute with no political content, and the reason the argument repeats without destroying the union is that money also flows the other way through the market, the structural funds, and the agricultural programme, so a net payer can point to gains that do not appear in the budget line. The tempting answers call the sums trivial, invent a payer veto, and deny the periodic agreements that exist precisely to revise the payments.
questions.hint: Ask what a net payer receives that does not appear on the budget's own accounts.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Support prices, storage, and the rising cost of the farm policy
questions.learningObjective: read a budget series as a price-support consequence
questions.stem: A table for the 1980s shows farm prices held above world prices, storage rising year after year, and a growing share of the budget going to storage and disposal. What best explains the growing cost?

options.text: Holding prices above world rates creates surpluses, so the budget pays to store unsold produce

options.misconception: claims world prices collapsed, which the same table contradicts on every row
options.text: World prices fell to nothing, so the budget grew only because storage became unusually expensive

options.misconception: assumes a shortfall, where a price floor is precisely a promise not to allow one
options.text: Farmers produced less than the market wanted, so the gap was filled by a new storage line

options.misconception: reverses the direction of the share the table shows rising in every year
options.text: The share going to storage fell every year, so the rising cost came from a shrinking share

questions.explanation: A price held above the world level invites production beyond what buyers will take, and the difference between what is produced and what is bought has to go somewhere, so it goes into store, and a growing store and a growing storage line in the budget are the same fact seen twice. The tempting answers collapse world prices, describe a shortfall that a price floor prevents, and reverse a share the table shows rising in every year.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to output when a floor keeps the price above the world level.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A large state trading freely but not a member
questions.learningObjective: recall what sets the size of the obstacle to membership
questions.stem: One large state has been a candidate for membership since 1999 while trading freely with the union and not being a member of it. What sets the size of the obstacle it faces?

options.text: The union's own entry conditions, which the candidate must meet on the rule of law and government

options.misconception: assumes duties still apply under a customs union, which removes them by design
options.text: The customs duties its traders still pay, since a customs union would not lift them for years yet

options.misconception: makes neighbouring armies an entry criterion, which the criteria never included
options.text: The strength of the armies around it, which the union weighs before opening talks with any state

options.misconception: invents a size limit the treaties contain no trace of
options.text: Its population, since the union's rules bar any state larger than a fixed size from joining

questions.explanation: The state has already done the part that trade can do, since the customs union gives its exporters the same access the members enjoy, so the remaining obstacle cannot be economic and must be the union's stated political conditions on government, courts, and rule of law, which is why candidacy can sit open for years without closing. The tempting answers invent duties that the customs arrangement lifted, neighbouring armies, and a size limit no treaty contains.
questions.hint: Ask what the candidate already has and what it therefore cannot be short of.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A rich state that stays outside
questions.learningObjective: recall why one European state declined membership
questions.stem: A rich state inside the continent has stayed outside the union and outside the common currency while keeping close economic ties with its neighbours. What best explains that choice?

options.text: Its neutrality and its own legal rules mattered more, and membership required both to be given up

options.misconception: calls the economy small, which the state's prosperity plainly contradicts
options.text: Its economy was too small to gain, since the single market only matters for large industrial states

options.misconception: assumes an application refused, which the state's own choices contradict
options.text: It applied and was refused, so the state settled for trade agreements rather than membership

options.misconception: makes leaving the customs union a condition of the neutrality it valued
options.text: Neutrality was lost by entering the customs union, so the state had to reject trade as well

questions.explanation: Membership asks a state to accept a legal order it did not write, to take decisions by a rule rather than by its own law, and to place monetary policy in hands it does not control, and where a state's own constitution and tradition make that unacceptable, staying out while trading freely is the coherent answer rather than a failure to modernise. The tempting answers call a rich economy small, invent a refused application, and make the customs union the thing that would have cost the neutrality.
questions.hint: Ask what the state would have to accept in law and in money on joining.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Accepting both the old money and the new
questions.learningObjective: recall why a currency change allowed both notes to circulate
questions.stem: When the common currency replaced national money in 2002, shops in most member states were required for a time to accept both the new and the old. What was the point of that double acceptance?

options.text: A legal change is only usable if the old note still works, or the swap would stop every purchase

options.misconception: asserts a currency-setting power that a single currency removes by definition
options.text: It allowed the common currency to set a rate, since two prices could be quoted for one sum

options.misconception: assumes continued national issue, which the introduction of one money ended
options.text: It kept the national currencies in use, since states were still allowed to issue their own

options.misconception: converts a transition rule into a source of revenue for the issuers
options.text: It gave the banks two years of extra revenue, since both sets of notes were printed by the state

questions.explanation: A legal obligation is worthless to a trader who cannot make a sale on the day it takes effect, so requiring both to be accepted removes the only reason a person would keep the old note instead of changing, and it is that which turns a legal date into an actual change of money in circulation. The tempting answers invent a rate-setting power, an ongoing right to issue, and a windfall for the issuers, none of which the double acceptance created.
questions.hint: Ask what a shopkeeper would do with a customer who only has the old note.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Borrowing together after a shock closed every economy
questions.learningObjective: analyze why joint borrowing answered a shared shock
questions.stem: When a shock closed every economy in the union within weeks, the member states borrowed jointly for the first time and lent the money back rather than each supporting itself. Why was joint borrowing the workable answer?

options.text: The shock was shared, so no single state could borrow at rates the others could obtain alone

options.misconception: makes the shock local, which is what a common borrowing fund is not for
options.text: One member was hit far worse, so a common fund was needed to share the cost of that crisis

options.misconception: asserts a cheaper rate that borrowing for others does not by itself deliver
options.text: Common borrowing lowered the interest paid by firms, so the states pooled their debts for that

options.misconception: assumes a legal incapacity to borrow that the states' own constitutions allow
options.text: The states had no legal power to borrow, so the union had to borrow on their behalf instead

questions.explanation: Lenders decide who to fund by weighing the chance of repayment, and when every member's output falls at the same moment, the risk attached to any one of them rises with the whole bloc rather than with its own policy, so a borrower of average quality loses access precisely when it most needs funds, and a promise from the whole union is what keeps that door open. The tempting answers make the shock local, promise a cheaper rate for firms, and assume a legal incapacity to borrow that the states' own constitutions do not contain.
questions.hint: Ask how a lender judges one member's risk on a day when all members are failing.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A legal standard written into the budget rules
questions.learningObjective: analyze why enforcement was attached to money
questions.stem: In recent years the union has held back part of the shared budget from member states that weakened their courts or their audit offices, using a clause written into the budget rules. Why put the standard there rather than in a declaration?

options.text: The budget is the payment the union controls, so a standard can bite where a vote would fail

options.misconception: puts a political mechanism in the hands of judges, which is not how it works
options.text: The courts enforce the budget rules, so the standard is applied by judges rather than politicians

options.misconception: reverses the direction of the payment into a reward the rules never provided
options.text: The clause was added to reward good behaviour, so payments rise for states that comply with it

options.misconception: denies the binding force of a rule the states agreed and can change
options.text: The budget carries no legal force, so the clause is a statement of intent that binds no one

questions.explanation: A standard announced as a principle is answered with argument, while a standard written next to a payment changes the calculation in a finance ministry, so attaching the condition to money is the only place where a union without its own tax authority can make a rule bind anybody, and it explains why the clause had to be phrased in budget terms rather than in constitutional ones. The tempting answers give the courts the power, reverse the payment into a reward, and deny the force of a rule the member states themselves agreed.
questions.hint: Ask what a union that cannot tax can actually use to make a rule mean something.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where exports go before and after the single market
questions.learningObjective: read a trade share series as the effect of a customs union
questions.stem: A table of export shares from two years on either side of the single market shows exports to the other members rising sharply while each state's share going to the rest of the world falls. What does the pattern isolate?

options.text: The customs union's effect, since duties inside the group went and duties outside it stayed

options.misconception: credits a currency that had not yet been introduced at the time of the change
options.text: The common currency's effect, since one money is the only thing that raises trade between states

options.misconception: explains a share changing by a rise in exports everywhere, which is a different pattern
options.text: A general rise in world trade, since every state sold more abroad and the group share followed

options.misconception: infers falling output from a falling share, which is not what a share measures
options.text: A fall in total output, since losing export markets shrank every industry that had supplied them

questions.explanation: A share is a ratio, and the interesting fact is that the two directions moved in opposite ways at the same moment: more sales to the neighbours and a smaller proportion going outside, which is what removing duties at the internal border while leaving the external one standing must look like, since firms redirect effort toward the market that has just become cheaper to reach. The tempting answers credit a common currency that did not yet exist, claim a general rise in world trade, and read a falling share as falling output, which a share cannot show.
questions.hint: Ask which border's duty changed and which one did not.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two accounts of how the union grew
questions.learningObjective: synthesize pressure and consent as causes of institutional change
questions.stem: Two original summaries of the union's growth disagree: one says crises forced governments to pool powers before they would otherwise have moved, the other says the pooling was a political choice made in calm years and then defended by those who benefited. Which synthesis fits both?

options.text: Crises supplied the pressure and party choice supplied the consent, so the two belong in one account

options.misconception: keeps only the pressure, which is what the second summary's consent claim denies
options.text: Only the crises matter, since a political choice would have been reversed before the first deadline

options.misconception: keeps only the consent, which is what the first summary's pressure claim denies
options.text: Only the party choice matters, since the crises left the union with nothing that needed an answer

options.misconception: calls the two incompatible when they can both be true of different steps
options.text: The two are incompatible, since pooling powers and delaying decisions cannot occur in one decade

questions.explanation: A crisis supplies the reason to move and the party supplies the majority that ratifies, so the steps that matter in the record are the ones where both were present, and reading either half alone either overstates external compulsion or overstates the freedom of choice, which the delays and the reversals in the record contradict. The tempting answers keep one half and discard the other, and the last treats two descriptions of different steps as a contradiction.
questions.hint: Ask what a crisis supplies that a party cannot, and what a party supplies that a crisis cannot.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A handful of states remove routine checks on people
questions.learningObjective: recall what an internal frontier agreement abolished
questions.stem: An agreement signed in 1985 by a handful of states removed routine passport checks at the borders they shared, and more states joined it afterwards. What did that agreement actually abolish?

options.text: Checks on people at the internal frontiers, leaving the checks on goods outside them in place

options.misconception: extends the agreement to customs controls it deliberately left with the community
options.text: Every border control, since the agreement also ended the inspection of goods entering the group

options.misconception: turns a passport agreement into a monetary one, which came in a later separate step
options.text: The national currencies, since a common border was meant to be the first step towards one money

options.misconception: assumes a military reading of a civil agreement about travel documents
options.text: The military borders, since the signatories agreed to withdraw the troops along their frontier

questions.explanation: Two states that abolish checks on their own citizens between them have settled a question about movement that customs had never covered, and leaving the external checks in place preserves the common protection the group depends on, which is why the agreement spread to more states as a sign of trust rather than as a customs measure. The tempting answers extend it to goods, convert it into a currency step, and read it as a military arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two kinds of border check the signatories were entitled to control themselves.
